Assume the SLO is 99.9% availability over a rolling 30-day window. That gives a 0.1% error budget—43 minutes 12 seconds of equivalent total outage per 30 days.

The core policy should be:

> Page only for ongoing customer impact that is rapidly consuming the error budget, or when the independent mechanism needed to detect an outage has failed. Everything else becomes a ticket, dashboard signal, or automated remediation.

## Define the availability signal correctly

Measure at the public service edge, as close to the customer as possible:

- Total events: valid customer operations.
- Bad events: 5xx responses, gateway failures, server-side timeouts, capacity-related 429s, and responses exceeding the availability deadline.
- Exclude invalid client requests such as malformed requests and failed authentication.
- Count the final customer-visible result, not every internal retry.
- Maintain separate SLIs for important journeys that a global average could hide, such as login, reads, writes, or checkout.
- Evaluate globally and for customer-significant regions, but never per pod or host.

If latency matters independently, give it a separate latency SLO rather than mixing arbitrary latency thresholds into availability.

## What pages

Use multi-window, multi-burn-rate alerting. For a 99.9% SLO:

\[
\text{burn rate}=\frac{\text{observed bad-event ratio}}{0.001}
\]

Page when either pair below is true:

| Page condition | Long window | Short window | Bad-event threshold | Budget consumed |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Fast burn | 1 hour | 5 minutes | Both exceed 1.44% | 2% |
| Sustained burn | 6 hours | 30 minutes | Both exceed 0.60% | 5% |

In rule form:

```text
page =
  (burn_rate_1h > 14.4 AND burn_rate_5m > 14.4)
  OR
  (burn_rate_6h > 6 AND burn_rate_30m > 6)
```

The long window establishes significance; the short window proves the problem is still happening. A total outage should cross the fast-burn condition in roughly one minute, subject to metric and evaluation delay. These are the established starting thresholds recommended by Google’s SRE guidance. [Google SRE Workbook: Alerting on SLOs](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/)

Also page for:

- **Confirmed black-box outage:** public DNS/TLS plus a representative request checked every 30 seconds from three independent locations; page when at least two locations fail three consecutive checks. A single-location failure opens a ticket.
- **Alerting blind spot:** an independent dead-man check says the metrics or paging pipeline has been unable to detect/report service outages for more than five minutes. Route this to the monitoring/platform on-call, not the web-service on-call.
- **Exceptional deterministic imminent outage:** only when failure will occur before staffed hours and there is an immediate mitigation—for example, certificate expiry within four hours after automated renewal has failed. This exception should be rare and reviewed individually.

Do not add a separate page for CPU, memory, pod restarts, database connections, or the suspected dependency when an SLO page is already firing.

## What only opens a ticket

| Ticket condition | Long window | Short window | Bad-event threshold | Response expectation |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Elevated burn | 24 hours | 2 hours | Both exceed 0.30% / 3× burn | Next business day |
| Budget leak | 3 days | 6 hours | Both exceed 0.10% / 1× burn | Within three business days |

```text
ticket =
  (burn_rate_24h > 3 AND burn_rate_2h > 3)
  OR
  (burn_rate_3d > 1 AND burn_rate_6h > 1)
```

Both conditions consume approximately 10% of the 30-day budget before firing. They identify problems that matter but do not require somebody to wake up.

These should also be tickets, not pages:

- One failed synthetic location.
- A single unhealthy instance, pod, zone, or replica while redundancy works.
- CPU, memory, disk, connection-pool, queue, or autoscaling pressure without SLO impact.
- Traffic anomalies without confirmed failures.
- Deployment failures that rolled back cleanly.
- Error spikes that have already recovered.
- Certificate expiry beyond the emergency window.
- Loss of redundancy or projected capacity exhaustion days away.
- Telemetry missing while independent synthetic checks remain healthy.

A one-interval synthetic or total-error event should automatically create an incident record even if it recovers before paging. This preserves evidence of brief real outages without waking someone after there is no longer an action to take.

## Prevent notification multiplication

One outage should produce one incident and normally one initial page:

- Group by `service + environment + SLO`, not instance, endpoint, exception, or region.
- Deduplicate the fast- and sustained-burn rules into the same incident.
- Suppress pod, dependency, and capacity notifications while the service-impact page is active.
- Inhibit downstream-service alerts when a confirmed shared dependency incident explains them.
- Escalate an unacknowledged page after 5 and 10 minutes; do not send repeated “new” pages for the same incident.
- Keep the alert active for about five minutes after recovery to prevent flapping, but mark recovery in the same incident.

Prometheus similarly recommends paging on user-visible symptoms and keeping cause-based alerts for diagnosis or non-urgent handling. [Prometheus alerting practices](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/alerting/)

Every page must contain:

- The customer impact and affected journey/region.
- Current short- and long-window burn rates.
- Approximate budget consumption.
- Dashboard and runbook links.
- Recent deployments/configuration changes.
- A concrete first action: rollback, fail over, shed load, or invoke a named dependency.

If the recipient cannot take a useful action immediately, it is not a page.

## Low-traffic protection

Ratio alerts become noisy when one failed request represents a large percentage. For low-volume slices:

- Require an agreed minimum number of bad operations before a ratio-based page—for example, 20 affected operations—unless black-box checks confirm an outage.
- Derive that number from the smallest customer impact the business considers wake-worthy; do not treat 20 as universal.
- Rely on multi-location synthetic transactions for complete or near-complete outages.
- Route ratio crossings below the minimum sample size to tickets.

This avoids paging for one failed request while preserving outage detection.

## Rollout and verification

Replay the new rules against at least 30–90 days of historical data, including last week:

1. Confirm that all three real incidents would have generated a page before or no later than the first useful existing page.
2. Confirm that the other 37 notifications become tickets, dashboard signals, or are eliminated.
3. Shadow the new routing for two weeks while retaining the old alerts as non-paging comparisons.
4. Require every paging rule to demonstrate an actionable incident at review; otherwise demote or remove it.
5. Test quarterly with synthetic DNS, TLS, 5xx, timeout, regional, and telemetry-loss scenarios.

The likely outcome for last week would be about three deduplicated incident pages—not 40—while brief self-healed failures and infrastructure warnings remain recorded and assigned without interrupting the on-call.
results.notes: Solid, correctly derived thresholds and sensible page/ticket split with citations, but thinner on implementation detail (no full alerting config) and less rigorous on edge cases like traffic collapse.

# Caching Strategy for a Price-Sensitive Catalog API (2-Second Freshness Bound)

## Decision

1. **Split data by volatility.** Descriptive product data (title, images, specs) gets long CDN TTLs and tag-based purge. Prices get their own endpoint.
2. **Give prices a 1-second shared-cache TTL**, with no stale serving, cached at **one** CDN tier.
3. **Keep Redis current with versioned upserts**, driven by a durable change stream (CDC or transactional outbox). The app may also write immediately after commit to cut latency.
4. **Let TTL arithmetic enforce the 2-second bound.** Purges and the app's direct write only make updates arrive sooner. If any of them silently fails, the TTLs still cap staleness.
5. **Checkout always re-prices from the primary DB.** The 2-second bound is a display SLO, not a charging guarantee.

The workload fits this design. 10k reads/s against 5 writes/s is about 2000:1, so even a 1-second edge TTL absorbs most traffic. Five price updates per second is trivial for Redis.

---

## 1. Resource design

| Resource | Contents | Shared cache | Browser | Invalidation |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `GET /products/{id}` | Descriptive data, **no price** | `s-maxage=86400, stale-while-revalidate=60`, surrogate key `product-{id}` | short, e.g. `max-age=60` | Purge by tag on change; slow purges are harmless here |
| `GET /products/{id}/price` | `amount, currency, price_version` | `s-maxage=1`, **no SWR, no stale-if-error**, key `price-{id}` | `max-age=0` | TTL is the guarantee; tag purge is optional |

- **Prefer per-SKU price URLs as the cached unit.** A batch URL like `/prices?ids=…` fragments the cache across ID combinations.
  - If you need batching, sort the IDs, strip irrelevant query parameters and cookies, or compose at the edge.
  - The client or the edge (ESI or edge compute) merges product data and price.
- **Anything else that embeds prices inherits the price policy.** This includes listing, search, category pages and HTML. Either fetch prices through the price endpoint, or give those pages a 1-second TTL. This is the most common way the promise gets broken.
- **If you truly cannot split the resources,** the whole product response takes the price policy. It still works, but with a worse hit ratio.
- **Expose `price_version`** (e.g. an `X-Price-Version` header) so staleness can be debugged.

## 2. CDN layer (prices)

- **Headers:** `Cache-Control: public, max-age=0, s-maxage=1`.
- **Verify the CDN actually honors a 1-second TTL.** Some plans enforce minimum edge TTLs.
- **Cache prices at a single tier.** With an origin shield plus edge, TTLs stack: 1 s at the shield plus 1 s at the edge.
  - Honoring `Age` does not fully fix this, because `Age` is expressed in whole seconds.
  - Either cache at the shield and only pass through at the edge, or cache at the edge and only collapse requests at the shield.
- **Enable request collapsing.** Origin load is then at most about 1 request/s per hot SKU per caching location. Long-tail SKUs miss and go to Redis, which handles thousands of requests/s at sub-millisecond latency.
- **Purge on write only if it is fast and cheap on your CDN.**
  - Fastly and Cloudflare tag purges land in roughly 150 ms or less. Batch them every ~100 ms.
  - On CDNs with slow or per-path-billed invalidation, skip purging. CloudFront, for example, bills per path, and 5/s is about 430k invalidations per day.
  - The gain is small either way: at most about 1 s off typical staleness.

## 3. Redis layer

**Key:** `price:{sku}` → `{amount, currency, version}`. The version is the row version or commit LSN and must increase monotonically.

**Reliable write path (the guarantee):**
1. The price update commits. Either CDC (e.g. Debezium on the binlog or WAL) captures it, or an outbox row commits in the same transaction.
2. The change goes to a durable log (Kafka, Redis Streams).
3. A consumer runs an atomic Lua **set-if-newer** script, then optionally issues the CDN purge.

**Fast path (optional, best effort):** after commit, the app runs the same set-if-newer script. This brings typical commit-to-Redis time to about 10–50 ms. CDC covers any crash between the commit and this call.

**Why upsert rather than delete:** overwriting avoids a miss stampede on a hot SKU right after a price change.

**Why versioned:** plain cache-aside has a race.
1. A reader misses and loads the old price.
2. A writer commits and invalidates the key.
3. The reader writes the old price back, and it sticks.

With a version check, step 3 becomes a no-op. The same check protects against out-of-order CDC events.

**Read path on a miss:**
- Load the price from the **primary**, or from a replica only if its version or LSN is verified.
- Use single-flight per key so concurrent misses share one load.
- Write back with set-if-newer.

**Safety nets:**
- **Redis TTL:** about 10–30 minutes with jitter. This is for memory hygiene and bug containment only, not freshness.
- **Redis failover:** replication is asynchronous, so a failover can lose recent writes and resurrect old prices. On failover, do one of the following:
  - bump a namespace epoch (`price:v{epoch}:{sku}`), or
  - replay CDC from a safe offset.

## 4. Staleness budget (worst case, purge failed)

Staleness stacks: the edge may cache a response built from Redis just before the update landed.

| Component | Bound |
|---|---|
| Commit → Redis updated | ~50 ms via app path; ≤500 ms via CDC at p99 (alert at 500 ms) |
| CDN object age (single tier) | ≤1 s |
| In-flight request, clock and rounding slop | ~100–200 ms |
| **Total** | **≈1.2–1.7 s < 2 s** |

With a successful purge, typical time-to-fresh is about 200–400 ms.

## 5. Operating it

- **End-to-end SLI:** change a canary SKU's price every 30–60 s and poll it from several POPs and regions. Record time-to-fresh and alert if p99 exceeds 1.5 s.
- **Supporting alerts:**
  - CDC consumer lag,
  - app fast-path failures,
  - purge API errors or rate limiting,
  - spikes in rejected older-version writes.
- **Degraded mode:** if CDC lag breaches budget, a circuit breaker routes price reads past Redis to the primary, or to a lag-bounded replica.
  - Guard that path with a connection-pool or rate limit.
  - The 1-second CDN cache keeps shielding the origin meanwhile.
- **Origin outage:** show "price unavailable" rather than a stale price, unless the business explicitly accepts stale prices.

## 6. Authoritative paths

Cart totals and checkout re-read the price from the primary DB. If it changed, tell the user. Never charge from any cache.

---

## What I would NOT do

1. **Rely on long CDN TTLs plus purge-on-write.** Purges are asynchronous, best effort and rate-limited. They are sometimes slow (seconds on some vendors), sometimes expensive at about 430k per day, and they fail silently. When one is lost, staleness has no upper bound.
2. **Set the CDN price TTL to 2 s, or cache prices at both shield and edge.** Pipeline lag and stacked TTLs would breach the budget routinely.
3. **Use `stale-while-revalidate` or `stale-if-error` on prices.** Both serve content past the TTL by design. `stale-if-error` could show hours-old prices during an outage.
4. **Give browsers or intermediate proxies any `max-age` on prices.** They cannot be purged.
5. **Put prices inside long-cached product JSON, HTML, listing or search pages.**
6. **Rely on app dual-writes alone** ("update DB, then update or delete cache"). A crash or timeout between the steps loses the invalidation forever. Also never update the cache before commit or inside the transaction, because a rollback would leave a price in the cache that never existed.
7. **Use unversioned cache-aside:** delete then lazy refill, unconditional SET on miss, or refill from a lagging replica. Each reopens the stale-refill race. Double-delete-with-sleep is a hack, not a fix.
8. **Use a short Redis TTL (e.g. 1–2 s) as the freshness mechanism, or TTL-only expiry at every layer.** You get stacked staleness, constant misses and synchronized stampedes.
9. **Use Redis pub/sub for invalidation,** including for in-process L1 caches. It is at-most-once, so a dropped message leaves a node stale indefinitely. If you add L1 caches, cap their TTL at about 200–250 ms and count it in the budget.
10. **Use `FLUSHALL`, `KEYS`/`SCAN` + `DEL`, or wildcard or full CDN purges.** At 5 writes/s this would effectively disable caching and flood the origin at 10k RPS. Use explicit keys and surrogate tags.
11. **Treat the 2-second bound as a hard guarantee for money.** It is a display SLO; checkout re-prices from the DB.

---

### How the three drafts were reconciled

- **Primary Redis update path.** Draft 2 made the app write primary with CDC as backstop. Drafts 1 and 3 made CDC or outbox primary. The combined design makes CDC or outbox the guarantee and keeps the app write as a latency optimization. This keeps typical staleness low without depending on a non-atomic dual write.
- **Purge cost.** Draft 1 treated 5 purges/s as trivially fine. Draft 2 noted cost and rate limits on some CDNs. Both are true depending on the vendor, so purge is conditional. It also buys at most about 1 s under a 1-second TTL.
- **Tier stacking.** Honoring `Age` alone is weaker than caching at one tier, because `Age` has whole-second granularity. The answer therefore recommends a single tier.
- **Additions.** Two points appeared in only one draft and are kept because they close real holes:
  - the Redis failover epoch or replay (Draft 2),
  - listing and search pages embedding prices (Draft 1).
results.notes: Very thorough and specific (single-tier caching due to Age granularity, CDN purge cost realism, per-SKU URL guidance, degraded-mode handling); includes a slightly odd 'reconciliation of drafts' meta-section but otherwise high quality and accurate.

# Postgres FTS vs. a Dedicated Search Engine for 2M Documents with Filters and Sub-5-Second Freshness

## Decision

**Use a dedicated engine: OpenSearch or Elasticsearch. Keep Postgres as the source of truth and feed the engine through an outbox + queue pipeline.**

Postgres FTS is a legitimate choice at this size, and I'd pick it under the conditions listed at the end. For a SaaS product where search is a user-facing feature, a dedicated engine is the better long-term bet.

### Why not Postgres FTS

2M rows is not a scale problem for Postgres. The weak spots are search quality and certain query shapes:

| Concern | Postgres FTS | OpenSearch / Elasticsearch |
|---|---|---|
| Freshness | Immediate, since the index is updated in the same transaction | About 1 s refresh plus pipeline lag, so 1–3 s is realistic |
| Relevance | `ts_rank` has no corpus statistics (no IDF or BM25), so ranking is weak | BM25, field boosts, function scores, synonyms |
| Common-term queries | Ranking requires scoring every match, so a term matching 300k rows is slow | Top-k scoring with early termination |
| FTS combined with selective filters | The planner often picks badly between a GIN index and B-tree indexes | Filter clauses are cached bitsets and combine cheaply |
| Typo tolerance, prefix search, highlighting | Only partial, via `pg_trgm`, `:*` prefix matching and `ts_headline` (slow at scale) | Native support |
| Facet counts | `GROUP BY` over the match set, which gets expensive | Aggregations |
| Operational load | Nothing new to run | A cluster plus a pipeline to operate |

The real cost of the dedicated engine is **eventual consistency and a pipeline to maintain**. The rest of this answer is about making that pipeline correct.

### Why OpenSearch/Elasticsearch over Meilisearch or Typesense

- **Typesense** holds the index in RAM. With 2M documents that have real bodies, memory cost and capacity planning become a problem. It is excellent if documents are small.
- **Meilisearch** is great for relevance out of the box. However, indexing runs as asynchronous task batches, and under sustained heavy writes the task queue can push freshness past 5 s. Its analytics and aggregation features are also thinner.
- **OpenSearch/Elasticsearch** stores its index on disk and supports:
  - aggregations for facets;
  - external versioning, which makes writes idempotent;
  - index aliases for zero-downtime reindexing.

  Choose OpenSearch for a permissive license or AWS-managed hosting. Choose Elastic Cloud if you want Elastic's features. The pipeline below is the same for both.

---

## Indexing pipeline

```
 App write txn ──► Postgres: documents + outbox row (same txn)
                          │
                 Debezium (WAL / outbox router)  or  outbox poller
                          │
                 Kafka topic "doc-changes", keyed by document_id
                          │
                 Indexer workers (micro-batch, coalesce, fetch latest from PG)
                          │
                 _bulk API (version_type=external) ──► alias "docs" → index docs_v7
                          │
                 Failed items ──► retry with backoff ──► DLQ
```

### 1. Capture changes with a transactional outbox

Every write that affects search inserts an outbox row **in the same transaction** as the change:

```sql
INSERT INTO search_outbox (document_id, tenant_id, reason, created_at)
VALUES ($1, $2, 'updated', clock_timestamp());
```

- **Why an outbox instead of raw CDC on the `documents` table:** search documents are denormalized from several tables (tags, project, ACLs, author name). The application knows which document IDs a change affects, while raw table CDC would require join logic inside the pipeline.
- **Relay:** Debezium's outbox event router reads the outbox from the WAL, giving roughly 100–500 ms latency. A poller using `SELECT … FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` every 200 ms is a simpler alternative.
- **Cleanup:** delete outbox rows once relayed, or partition the table by day and drop old partitions.
- **Avoid fan-out:** model ACLs as principal or group IDs stored on the document. Adding a user to a group then changes no documents. Without this, one membership change can trigger reindexing of 100k documents.

### 2. Queue

- Use Kafka, or SQS FIFO / Redpanda.
- Partition by `document_id` so events for the same document stay ordered and workers scale horizontally.
- Events carry **only IDs**, not payloads.

### 3. Indexer workers

Each worker runs this loop:

1. **Consume a micro-batch.** Flush at 500 events or 200 ms, whichever comes first.
2. **Coalesce by `document_id`.** Ten edits to one document in 200 ms become one index operation.
3. **Fetch the current state from Postgres** in one query, joining the tables needed for denormalization. This is the key correctness choice:
   - Out-of-order or duplicate events become harmless, because the worker always writes the latest state.
   - If the row is gone or soft-deleted, the worker emits a `delete`.
   - Replaying the whole topic is safe.
4. **Build the search document:**
   - `id`, `tenant_id`
   - `title`, `body`
   - `tags`, `status`, `project_id`
   - `acl_principals[]`
   - `created_at`, `updated_at`
   - `version`: a `bigint` column incremented on every update, or `updated_at` in microseconds.
5. **Write with `_bulk`** using `version_type=external` and `version=<row version>`. A stale write loses with a 409 conflict, which is treated as success.
6. **Commit Kafka offsets only after the bulk response.** This gives at-least-once delivery, and step 3 makes it idempotent.
7. **Handle per-item errors:**
   - 429 or 5xx: retry with backoff and apply backpressure to consumption.
   - Mapping or parsing errors: send to the DLQ and alert.
   - Never fail the whole batch because of one item.

**Attachments** (PDF or DOCX text extraction) go through a **separate, slower stage**. Index metadata and body immediately, then issue a partial update when the extracted text is ready. Extraction can take longer than 5 s, and it should not consume the freshness budget of normal edits.

### 4. Index design

- **One shared index for all tenants, with `tenant_id` as a keyword filter.** Do not create an index per tenant; thousands of small indices hurt cluster stability.
- **Sizing:** assuming an average of about 20 KB of text per document, that is about 40 GB of source, so use 2–3 primary shards, 1 replica, and a 3-node cluster.
  - Custom routing by tenant is optional. Watch for hot shards if one tenant is very large.
- **Mappings:**
  - `dynamic: strict`;
  - `title` as `text` with a `keyword` subfield;
  - `body` with language analyzers;
  - `search_as_you_type` or an edge n-gram field for prefix search;
  - filter fields as `keyword` or `date`.
- **Settings:** `refresh_interval: 1s`. Do not use `refresh=wait_for` on every write, because it collapses throughput. For "I just saved it and don't see it" cases, insert the item optimistically in the UI.

### 5. Query side

- Build every query as a `bool` query:
  - `must` holds the `multi_match` with boosts;
  - `filter` holds `tenant_id`, `acl_principals` and the user's filters. Filters are cached and do not affect scoring.
- Inject the tenant and ACL filters **in a single server-side query builder**. Never take them from the client.
- Use `post_filter` so facet counts are not narrowed by the facet's own selection.
- Return IDs and highlights, then hydrate display data from Postgres or a cache. Optionally re-check permissions on the hydrated rows as defense in depth.

### 6. Freshness budget and monitoring

Rough p50 budget from commit to searchable:

| Stage | Time |
|---|---|
| Outbox relay | 0.3 s |
| Queue | <0.1 s |
| Batch wait | 0.2 s |
| Postgres fetch plus bulk | 0.2 s |
| Refresh | ≤1 s |
| **Total** | **about 1.5–2 s** |

That leaves headroom for p99 under 5 s.

Monitoring:

- **Lag metric:** time from outbox `created_at` to bulk acknowledgement, plus consumer group lag. Alert when p99 exceeds 3 s.
- **Synthetic canary:** every minute, write a canary document to a system tenant and measure the time until a search returns it. This is the true end-to-end SLA check.
- **Watch** for bulk rejections, DLQ depth and indexing latency.

### 7. Reconciliation

The pipeline will drift eventually, through bugs, manual SQL fixes, or restoring a Postgres backup.

- **Continuous:** re-enqueue documents whose `updated_at` falls in a sliding window, for example the last 24 hours, compared against index versions.
- **Nightly:** compare per-tenant counts and a checksum of `(id, version)` between Postgres and the index, then enqueue any mismatches.
- **Admin tool:** "reindex tenant X" simply enqueues that tenant's IDs.

### 8. Full reindex and mapping changes (zero downtime)

1. Create `docs_v8` with the new mapping, `replicas: 0` and `refresh_interval: -1`.
2. Record the current Kafka offset or outbox position.
3. Backfill from Postgres:
   - Use keyset pagination on `id` and run workers in parallel against the same `_bulk` path.
   - At 5–10k docs/s, 2M documents take about 5–10 minutes.
4. Start a second consumer group, replaying from the recorded position into `docs_v8`. Live writes continue into `docs_v7`, and external versions keep both indices correct.
5. Restore replicas and a 1 s refresh on `docs_v8`, wait for a green cluster, and run validation with count checks and sampled query comparisons.
6. Atomically swap the `docs` alias to `docs_v8`. Keep `docs_v7` for rollback, then delete it.

---

## When I would choose Postgres FTS instead

Choose Postgres if **most** of these are true:

- Search is a secondary feature, such as internal or admin search.
- There is exact-keyword matching in one or two languages, with no typo tolerance.
- Queries are always scoped to a tenant whose document count is small, say a few thousand to tens of thousands.
- Filters are simple and there are no facet counts.
- The team cannot take on running a cluster and a pipeline.

Implementation in that case:

- A `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (setweight(to_tsvector(...title), 'A') || setweight(to_tsvector(...body), 'B')) STORED` column.
- A GIN index on that column, plus B-tree indexes on `(tenant_id, …)`.
- `pg_trgm` for fuzzy title matching.
- Consider **ParadeDB `pg_search`**, which adds BM25 inside Postgres, as a middle path.

Freshness is then immediate and there is no pipeline. That is the real reason to choose it.
results.notes: Competent OpenSearch pipeline with reasonable freshness budget and reconciliation, but less depth on correctness edge cases (tombstones, ACL fan-out, chunking) than the strongest answers.

Assume the SLO is **99.9% over a rolling 30-day window**. That gives a 0.1% error budget—equivalent to 43.2 minutes of complete unavailability. The core change is to page on user-visible error-budget burn, not on individual machine or resource symptoms.

### What pages

Use the availability SLI:

```text
bad_ratio = bad eligible requests / all eligible requests
burn_rate = bad_ratio / 0.001
```

“Bad” should include server errors, timeouts, connection failures, and requests slower than the availability cutoff. Exclude client-caused failures such as valid 4xx responses. Measure at the user-facing edge so DNS, TLS, load balancer, and application failures are represented.

Create two page conditions, each requiring both its long and short window:

| Page | Condition | Equivalent bad-request rate | Why |
|---|---|---:|---|
| Fast burn | burn > 14.4 over both 1h and 5m | >1.44% | Detects severe outages quickly; consumes about 2% of the monthly budget in an hour |
| Sustained burn | burn > 6 over both 6h and 30m | >0.60% | Detects slower but still urgent incidents; consumes about 5% of the budget in six hours |

In pseudocode:

```text
PAGE if
  (bad_ratio_1h  > 0.0144 AND bad_ratio_5m  > 0.0144)
  OR
  (bad_ratio_6h  > 0.0060 AND bad_ratio_30m > 0.0060)
```

These are the standard multi-window, multi-burn-rate starting points recommended by Google SRE. Requiring the short window prevents paging for an incident that has already stopped, while the long window filters transient spikes. A complete outage should cross the fast-burn condition in roughly one minute, depending on evaluation frequency. [Google SRE Workbook](https://sre.google/workbook/alerting-on-slos/)

Add one independent outage detector for failures that request telemetry might miss:

```text
PAGE if at least 2 of 3 external probe regions
fail the critical transaction for 3 consecutive probes
```

Probe DNS resolution, TLS, the homepage or healthful read, and one representative authenticated operation if practical. Deduplicate this with the burn alert so one outage creates one incident, not two pages. If normal traffic is high enough, the SLO page remains authoritative; the probe is a telemetry and network-path backstop.

A page must contain:

- Current burn rate and user-visible failure rate.
- Affected regions, operations, and estimated traffic.
- Links to the SLO dashboard, recent deployments, dependencies, and runbook.
- A safe first action: rollback, fail over, shed load, or escalate.
- One incident key such as `service + SLO`, so regional, instance, fast-burn, and slow-burn signals group into one page.

### What opens a ticket

Use slow-burn conditions for work that matters but does not justify waking someone:

```text
TICKET if
  (burn > 3 over both 24h and 2h)
  OR
  (burn > 1 over both 3d and 6h)
```

For a 99.9% SLO, those are:

- More than 0.30% bad requests over both 24h and 2h.
- More than 0.10% bad requests over both three days and six hours.

Each represents roughly 10% of the monthly error budget consumed over its long window. The ticket should be due within one business day, assigned to the owning team, and include the same diagnostic context as a page.

The following should also be tickets—or dashboard signals if no concrete action exists—not pages:

- High CPU, memory, disk, connection count, or queue depth while the SLI remains healthy.
- A single failed instance, pod restart, replica loss, or unhealthy availability zone when redundancy is still intact.
- Dependency errors that have not caused user-visible SLI burn.
- Capacity warnings based on forecasted exhaustion.
- Certificate, quota, or disk warnings with adequate lead time.
- Monitoring gaps when an independent external signal still confirms service health.
- Batch-job or backup failures that do not threaten the availability SLO.

Set these thresholds from response time, not folklore such as “page at 80% CPU.” For example, if quota expansion takes three business days, create a ticket when conservative usage forecasting shows fewer than seven days remaining. If capacity collapses before the team can respond, automation or additional headroom is needed; turning it into a pager threshold is not a durable fix.

Prometheus similarly recommends paging on symptoms, using cause-level metrics for diagnosis, and avoiding pages where no immediate action exists. [Prometheus alerting practices](https://prometheus.io/docs/practices/alerting/)

### How the thresholds are derived

For reporting period \(T\), long alert window \(W\), and chosen budget fraction \(p\):

```text
burn threshold = p × T / W
error-rate threshold = burn threshold × (1 − SLO)
```

With \(T=720h\):

- \(2\% × 720 / 1 = 14.4\)
- \(5\% × 720 / 6 = 6\)
- \(10\% × 720 / 24 = 3\)
- \(10\% × 720 / 72 = 1\)

Use a short window approximately 1/12 of the long window and require both. If the organization uses a 28-day SLO window, recalculate rather than copying the 30-day values.

For low-traffic endpoints, percentage alerts become statistically noisy. Do not let one failed request page someone. Aggregate related operations, lengthen the windows, and rely on multi-region synthetic probes for total-outage detection. Keep separate SLIs only where the user impact or response genuinely differs.

### Rollout and noise controls

Before enabling paging:

1. Replay these rules over at least the previous 30–90 days.
2. Confirm they would have detected all three real incidents early enough to mitigate them.
3. Run them in shadow mode for two weeks.
4. Group all simultaneous symptoms into one incident.
5. Remove or downgrade the existing component alerts only after verifying coverage.
6. Review every page: if no immediate human action was required, downgrade, delete, or redesign it.

The operating target is approximately **one page per real incident**, not one page per failed component. The multi-window pages preserve detection of fast and gradual outages; external probes cover edge and telemetry blind spots; everything that can wait becomes scheduled work rather than an interruption.
results.notes: Correct core math and reasonable page/ticket split, but less specific on low-traffic guards, no full implementation, and thinner treatment of traffic-loss/blind-spot scenarios than the top answers.

# Search for 2M Documents: Postgres FTS vs. a Dedicated Engine

## Recommendation

**Use a dedicated engine: OpenSearch, or Elasticsearch, which is equivalent for this purpose.** Keep Postgres as the source of truth and feed the engine through an asynchronous, rebuildable indexing pipeline. A realistic end-to-end freshness target is p99 of about 2–3 s, which fits the 5 s budget.

One caveat first. 2M documents is not large, and Postgres full-text search can handle it. The deciding factor is **what "search" means to your users**, not the document count.

## 1. Decision reasoning

### Where Postgres FTS is fine
- **Freshness is free.** A generated `tsvector` column with a GIN index is transactional, so it has zero lag and no sync pipeline.
- **Filters are easy.** Use `WHERE tenant_id = … AND status = …` with `btree_gin` composite indexes.
- **Tenant scoping helps a lot.** If queries always filter to one tenant and tenants are small, each query only touches a few thousand rows.
- **Operations stay simple.** There is one system, no dual-write problem, and row-level security applies to search too.

### Where Postgres FTS breaks down
| Requirement | Postgres FTS | Dedicated engine |
|---|---|---|
| Relevance ranking | `ts_rank` has no BM25 and no corpus IDF. `ORDER BY ts_rank … LIMIT 20` must fetch and rank **every** matching row, so broad terms on large tenants take seconds. | BM25 with top-k pruning (WAND/block-max). |
| Typo tolerance / fuzzy | Needs `pg_trgm` as a separate mechanism, and combining it with FTS ranking is awkward. | Built in (`fuzziness`). |
| Search-as-you-type | Prefix `:*` only, with weak ranking. | edge n-grams, `search_as_you_type`. |
| Facet counts with filters | `GROUP BY` over the full match set, which is expensive and repeated per facet. | Aggregations over doc values. |
| Highlighting | `ts_headline` is slow because it re-parses documents. | Fast highlighters (offsets/postings). |
| Multi-language, synonyms, stemming | Per-config, clunky to mix. | Per-field analyzers, synonym graphs. |
| Load isolation | Search CPU and I/O compete with OLTP on the primary or replicas. | Separate cluster that scales independently. |

BM25 extensions exist (ParadeDB `pg_search`, `pg_textsearch`, VectorChord-bm25). However, they are often **unavailable on managed Postgres** (RDS, Cloud SQL) and add their own operational risk.

**Rule of thumb:**
- **Choose Postgres FTS** if all of these hold: search is keyword matching within a tenant, there are no facets or typo tolerance, tenants are small, and relevance is "good enough." In that case, stop reading and add a GIN index.
- **Choose a dedicated engine** if any of these hold: users expect product-grade search (typos, relevance, facets, autocomplete, highlighting), some tenants have hundreds of thousands of documents, or search load must not affect the primary database.

For a SaaS product explicitly asking for "full-text search with filters," the second case is almost always true. The 5 s freshness budget, rather than 0 s, also signals that an asynchronous pipeline is acceptable.

### Why OpenSearch/Elasticsearch over Meilisearch or Typesense
- **Typesense** is excellent and simple, with Raft-replicated HA. But its indexes are **RAM-bound**, and its query model is less flexible for complex boolean filters, document-level ACL term lists, and custom scoring. It is a good choice if your queries are simple and memory cost is acceptable.
- **Meilisearch** has great relevance and developer experience out of the box. However, writes go through an asynchronous task queue, and sustained high update rates on multi-million-document indexes have historically produced indexing lag that can exceed a strict 5 s SLA. It has improved considerably, so benchmark your actual write pattern if you prefer it.
- **OpenSearch/Elasticsearch** makes near-real-time a first-class property: the default `refresh_interval` of 1 s makes new writes searchable within about a second. It also offers mature bulk APIs, external versioning, aliases for zero-downtime reindexing, aggregations, and managed offerings. OpenSearch is Apache-2.0; Elasticsearch is available under AGPL/SSPL/ELv2.

## 2. Indexing pipeline

### Architecture
```
 App writes ──► Postgres (source of truth)
                   │  same transaction
                   ▼
            search_outbox table  ◄── triggers on documents, tags, acl, …
            (or Debezium CDC → Kafka, if you already run Kafka)
                   │
                   ▼
            Indexer workers (N, partitioned)
              1. claim batch (dedupe by doc_id)
              2. re-read current state from Postgres (bulk)
              3. build denormalized JSON
              4. _bulk index/delete with external version
                   │
                   ▼
            OpenSearch  write-alias → docs_v7   (refresh_interval: 1s)
                        read-alias  → docs_v7
                   ▲
 Search API ───────┘  (enforces tenant + ACL filters, optionally hydrates from Postgres)
```

### 2.1 Change capture: never dual-write from the app
Writing to Postgres and then to the engine loses updates on crashes and reorders them under concurrency. Use one of these instead:

- **Default for this scale: an outbox table populated by triggers.**
  ```sql
  CREATE TABLE search_outbox (
    id          bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
    doc_id      uuid NOT NULL,
    tenant_id   uuid NOT NULL,
    priority    smallint NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,   -- 0 = realtime, 1 = bulk fan-out
    created_at  timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
  );
  ```
  - Triggers on `documents` and on every table that contributes to the indexed document (tags, ACLs, author name) insert `doc_id` in the same transaction.
  - Triggers also catch writes from migrations, admin SQL, and backfills, which app-emitted events would miss.
- **Alternative: logical-replication CDC** (Debezium → Kafka, or a lighter tool such as Sequin or pgstream). This is preferable if you already operate Kafka or have a high write rate (thousands of changes per second). Partition by `doc_id` so updates to one document stay ordered.

### 2.2 Events are signals; always re-read current state
The event carries only "doc X changed." The worker fetches the **current** row set from Postgres and indexes that. This design has three benefits:
- **It is idempotent and convergent.** Duplicate or out-of-order events produce the correct final state.
- **Coalescing is free.** Ten edits in 300 ms become one index operation.
- **Deletes are unambiguous.** If the row is not found or is soft-deleted, the worker emits a delete.

### 2.3 Worker loop
```sql
-- claim a batch without blocking other workers
DELETE FROM search_outbox
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM search_outbox
  WHERE priority = 0
  ORDER BY id
  LIMIT 500
  FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
RETURNING doc_id;
```

1. **Batch.** Take up to 500 docs or wait 200–500 ms, whichever comes first, and dedupe `doc_id`s.
   - Only delete outbox rows after a successful bulk request. Alternatively, mark them in-flight and delete on success, so a crashed worker's batch is retried.
2. **Fetch.** Run one query, `WHERE d.id = ANY($1)`, joining tags, ACL, and author, to build the documents.
3. **Bulk write.** Send `_bulk` with `index` or `delete` actions, `version_type=external`, and `version` = a monotonically increasing `documents.version bigint`, bumped by trigger on any contributing change. Stale writes are then rejected with a 409.
4. **Handle each item's result:**
   - `409 version_conflict` → ignore, because a newer version is already indexed.
   - `429` or rejected execution → exponential backoff and retry the item.
   - Mapping or parse errors → send to a dead-letter table with the error, and alert.
5. **Scale.** Run N workers. At 2M docs and typical SaaS write rates, 2–4 workers are plenty.

### 2.4 Protect the SLA from fan-out
Some changes affect many documents at once, such as renaming a tag used by 80k docs or changing a group's membership. They enqueue many events at `priority = 1`, which a separate worker pool drains at a throttled rate. Real-time edits (`priority = 0`) are never stuck behind a bulk job.

### 2.5 Latency budget (p99)
| Stage | Target |
|---|---|
| Commit → outbox claim (poll every 100–250 ms, or CDC lag) | ≤ 0.5 s |
| Batch window | ≤ 0.5 s |
| Postgres fetch + `_bulk` | ≤ 0.5 s |
| OpenSearch refresh | ≤ 1 s |
| **Total** | **~2.5 s**, alert at 4 s |

- **Don't lower `refresh_interval` below 1 s.** It hurts indexing throughput and segment merging.
- **Don't use `refresh=true` on writes.** For read-your-own-writes in the editing UI, either use `refresh=wait_for` on that single user-initiated write only, or update the UI optimistically.

### 2.6 Index design
- **Mapping:** explicit, with `"dynamic": "strict"`.
  - `tenant_id`, `status`, `type`, `acl_principals` → `keyword` (filters, facets).
  - `title`, `body` → `text` with language analyzers. Give `title` a `search_as_you_type` or edge-n-gram subfield and a `keyword` subfield for sorting.
  - `created_at`, `updated_at` → `date`.
  - Disable `_source` fields you never return, or exclude large bodies from `_source` if you hydrate from Postgres.
- **Queries:** put all filters in `bool.filter`. Filters are non-scoring and cacheable, and the tenant and ACL filters are **always injected server-side** by the Search API. The engine is never exposed directly to clients.
- **Sizing:** with ~2M docs at ~5–10 KB of text, expect roughly 10–40 GB of primary index.
  - Use 2–3 primary shards (aim for 10–50 GB per shard) with 1 replica on a 3-node cluster.
  - Don't over-shard; it is the most common mistake at this scale.
- **Multi-tenancy:** use a single shared index with `tenant_id` filtering.
  - Custom `routing=tenant_id` improves query locality. Add `routing_partition_size` or give very large tenants their own index to avoid hot shards.

### 2.7 Backfills and mapping changes (zero downtime)
1. Create `docs_v8` with the new mapping, `refresh_interval: -1`, and `number_of_replicas: 0`.
2. Point the **write path at both** `docs_v7` and `docs_v8`: workers write to both during migration. Alternatively, record the outbox id or CDC LSN before the backfill and replay from it afterward.
3. Backfill from Postgres using keyset pagination (`WHERE id > $last ORDER BY id LIMIT 5000`), running parallel id-range workers against a read replica.
   - At ~5–10k docs/s, 2M docs takes about 5 minutes.
4. Restore the refresh interval and replicas, then wait for green status.
5. Validate per-tenant document counts and sample queries.
6. Atomically swap the read alias to `docs_v8`, stop dual-writing, and delete `docs_v7` later.

Because the index can always be rebuilt from Postgres, this same procedure is your disaster recovery. Snapshots only make recovery faster.

### 2.8 Correctness and observability
- **Deletes:** external-version delete tombstones are garbage-collected after `index.gc_deletes` (60 s). A very late stale write could resurrect a deleted document. The "re-read from Postgres" rule makes this self-healing on the next event, and reconciliation catches the rest.
- **Reconciliation job:** run nightly, or hourly per active tenant. Compare `(id, version)` sets or per-tenant count and checksum between Postgres and the index, then enqueue repairs.
- **Result hydration:** have search return IDs, scores, and highlights, then load display data from Postgres and re-check permissions. A document deleted or unshared within the last second then never leaks.
- **Metrics:**
  - Outbox depth and age of oldest row, per priority.
  - Bulk latency and per-item error rates.
  - Dead-letter count.
  - Cluster health, heap usage, and search/indexing latency.
- **Canary for true end-to-end freshness:** every minute, update a sentinel document in Postgres and poll search until it appears. Alert if the time exceeds 4 s. This one metric proves the 5 s SLA and catches failures that component metrics miss.

## Summary
- **Engine:** choose OpenSearch or Elasticsearch, because users of a SaaS product expect relevance, typo tolerance, facets, and highlighting, and Postgres FTS handles these poorly on large tenants.
- **Pipeline:** trigger-fed outbox (or CDC) → idempotent workers that coalesce events and re-read current state → `_bulk` with external versions → 1 s refresh.
  - Separate the real-time and fan-out lanes.
  - Use aliases for zero-downtime reindexing.
  - Reconcile against Postgres regularly.
  - Measure freshness with a canary.
- **When to reverse the decision:** if search requirements turn out to be simple tenant-scoped keyword matching, Postgres FTS with a GIN index is the better choice, because it removes the whole pipeline.
results.notes: Well-reasoned OpenSearch recommendation with a clear decision table, priority lanes, freshness budget, canary probe, and zero-downtime reindex/reconciliation procedures; comprehensive and accurate.

# Alerting Redesign for a Web Service with a 99.9% Availability SLO

## The core idea

37 of your 40 pages were noise, so only 7.5% were real. That almost always comes from four habits:

- **Paging on causes rather than symptoms.** CPU, pod restarts and queue depth fire often, while users are usually fine.
- **Per-instance alerts.** One bad host pages even though the load balancer routes around it.
- **Static thresholds with short windows.** A "1% errors for 5 min" rule pages on blips and still misses slow degradation.
- **No deduplication.** One incident turns into 5–10 pages.

The redesign has four parts:

1. **Page only on user-visible symptoms.** Measure them as error-budget burn rate, using multiwindow, multi-burn-rate alerts (Google SRE Workbook).
2. **Add a few backstops** for failures the burn-rate math can't see: traffic never arriving, or monitoring itself being dead.
3. **Turn causes and slow problems into tickets.**
4. **Delete or dashboard everything else.**

### The admission test for any page

An alert may page only if **all four** of these are true:

1. Users are affected now, or will be within hours with no automatic recovery.
2. A human must act now; it can't wait until morning.
3. Someone can act on it: there is a runbook, and on-call has access.
4. No other page already fires for the same failure.

If any condition fails, the alert becomes a ticket, a dashboard, or is deleted. Write this into your alerting policy.

---

## 1. Define the SLI correctly

Burn-rate alerts are only as good as the SLI behind them.

**SLI = bad requests / valid requests, over a rolling 30 days.**

- **Where to measure:** at the edge, meaning the load balancer, ingress or CDN logs. The app can't count requests that never reached it.
- **Valid requests:** real user traffic. Exclude health checks, synthetic probes, and known bots or scanners.
- **Bad requests:**
  - 5xx responses, LB or gateway timeouts, and connection resets.
  - 429s produced by *your own* load shedding. Per-client quota 429s are not bad.
  - Requests slower than a hard ceiling, e.g. 2–5 s. A hung service that returns nothing is down, and a status-code-only SLI misses that.
- **Not bad:** other 4xx responses, which are client errors.
- **Critical journeys:** give login, checkout and key write APIs their **own SLI with the same alert rules**. Suppose checkout is 1% of traffic and fails completely. The global error rate is then only 1%, which is below the fast-page threshold. Limit this to the 2–4 journeys that matter; per-endpoint SLOs bring back the noise.
- **Latency (optional):** a separate latency SLO, e.g. 99% of requests under 500 ms, uses exactly the same math with a 1% budget.

## 2. Budget math and how thresholds are derived

- **Error budget:** 0.1% of requests over 30 days. That equals **43.2 minutes** of total outage.
- **Burn rate:** observed error ratio ÷ 0.001. A burn rate of 1 spends exactly the whole budget in 30 days.
- **Budget consumed** = burn rate × window hours ÷ 720.

To derive a threshold, pick how much budget you're willing to lose before waking someone. Then:

**burn rate = budget fraction × 720 ÷ long-window hours.**

For example, 2% × 720 ÷ 1 h = 14.4.

| Action | Long window | Short window | Burn rate | Error-ratio threshold | Budget spent when it fires |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PAGE** (fast) | 1 h | 5 m | 14.4 | > 1.44% | 2% |
| **PAGE** (medium) | 6 h | 30 m | 6 | > 0.6% | 5% |
| TICKET (slow) | 24 h | 2 h | 3 | > 0.3% | 10% |
| TICKET (chronic) | 72 h | 6 h | 1 | > 0.1% | 10% |

**Both windows must exceed the threshold.**
- **The long window gives significance.** A 30-second blip can't average 1.44% over an hour.
- **The short window makes the alert clear within minutes of recovery.** Without it, a fixed incident keeps firing for up to an hour, which is a major source of "already resolved" pages.

**Detection time** ≈ long window × (threshold ÷ actual error rate), plus about 1 minute of scrape and evaluation lag:

| Actual error rate | What fires | Time to fire |
|---|---|---|
| 100% (hard down) | Fast page | ~1–2 min |
| 10% | Fast page | ~9 min |
| 2% | Fast page | ~43 min (budget would be gone in ~36 h) |
| 1% | Medium page | ~3.6 h |
| 0.5% | Slow ticket | ~14 h (budget would last ~6 days) |
| 0.2% | Chronic ticket | ~1.5 days |

Real outages page in minutes. Small sustained leaks become tickets well before the budget runs out.

**A known consequence:** a full outage of only about 1 minute burns about 2.3% of the monthly budget, so it will page. That is correct for a 99.9% SLO. Do not "fix" it by adding a long `for:` clause or quietly raising burn rates. If frequent short blips are really acceptable, the SLO is wrong, so renegotiate it explicitly. If they aren't acceptable, the service needs reliability work.

---

## 3. What PAGES (the complete list)

### P1. Fast SLO burn
- **Condition:** error ratio > 1.44% over both 1 h and 5 m.
- **Applies to:** the global SLI and each critical-journey SLI.

### P2. Medium SLO burn
- **Condition:** error ratio > 0.6% over both 6 h and 30 m.
- **Inhibition:** suppressed while P1 fires for the same SLI.

**Low-traffic guard for P1 and P2.** At 3 a.m., 1 failure in 40 requests is a "2.5% error rate." Require a minimum number of bad events in the short window, e.g. ≥ 10 in 5 m for P1 and ≥ 20 in 30 m for P2. Tune these to your overnight volume. The guard means a total outage during near-zero traffic may not trip P1, so P3 must exist.

### P3. External synthetic probe failure
This covers traffic that never reaches your LB: DNS, CDN, an expired certificate, the LB itself, or a region outage. In those cases the error ratio is 0/0 or looks perfect.

- **What to probe:** real user paths such as homepage, login, and one read API that touches the primary datastore. Never a `/healthz` that always returns 200.
- **Where from:** ≥ 3 independent external locations, on infrastructure you don't share, every 30–60 s.
- **Page when:** ≥ 2 locations fail for 3 consecutive checks, giving ~3–4 min detection.
- **Single location failing ≥ 15 min:** ticket only. That is usually the probe's network.

### P4. Traffic collapse
Catches the case where the service is up and probes pass, but real users can't reach you. Examples are a broken client release, a regional DNS or CDN misroute, or a bad routing change.

- **Page when** valid request rate is < ~25% of the **median of the same time over the previous 3–4 weeks**, for 10 minutes.
- **Only when** that baseline exceeds an absolute floor, so quiet hours don't fire.
- **Why a multi-week median:** it avoids comparing against a week that itself had an incident. Holidays can still trip it.
- **Do not** make it depend on the probe also failing. The probe already pages for that case; P4 exists for when probes are green.
- **Backtest it.** If it's noisy, loosen the percentage before demoting it.

### P5. Monitoring is blind
- **Dead-man's switch:** an always-firing Watchdog alert heartbeats to an *external* service, which pages if the heartbeat stops for 10 min. Without it, a dead Prometheus or Alertmanager silently hides every outage.
- **Absent SLI data:** `absent()` or a zero-sample check on the LB request metric for 10 min.
- These should almost never fire.

### P6. Imminent, certain exhaustion (narrow on purpose)
- **Disk:** a stateful dependency you own is projected full in **< 4 h** (linear prediction over the last 6 h), with no auto-remediation.
- **Certificate:** a TLS certificate expires in **< 48 h**.

Each has an earlier ticket threshold (below). If one of these pages ever fires, the ticket process failed, so treat it as a bug in that process.

**Nothing else pages.**

---

## 4. What opens a TICKET

Tickets go to the owning team's queue, are deduplicated, have an owner, and are handled on business days. They never page.

| Ticket | Condition | Why it's not a page |
|---|---|---|
| Slow burn | > 0.3% over 24 h and 2 h | 10% of budget gone; days remain |
| Chronic burn | > 0.1% over 72 h and 6 h | Steady leak; planning-level urgency |
| Budget low | < 25% of 30-day budget remaining, or projected to run out before the window ends | Triggers the error-budget policy: slow risky deploys, prioritize reliability |
| Budget exhausted | ≤ 0% remaining | Release freeze or reliability work per policy |
| Redundancy lost | Instance, pod or AZ down, crash-looping, or failing health checks while the SLI is fine | Fix before the next failure; users are fine now |
| Capacity | Sustained utilization > 75–80% (CPU, memory, connection pools, file descriptors) at peak over several days; disk or quota projected full in < 7 days | Capacity planning |
| Certificate expiry | < 21 days | Renewal automation failed |
| Single-location probe failure | 1 location failing ≥ 15 min | Usually the probe network |
| Latency regression | p99 above baseline but below the SLI's hard ceiling | Early warning |
| Dependency degraded | Upstream errors or retries elevated, no SLO burn | Retries or fallbacks are absorbing it |
| Backlog or replication lag | Growing but not yet affecting the SLI | Investigate before it does |
| Backup, cron or pipeline failures | Job failed | Must be fixed, not at 3 a.m. |
| 4xx spike | Sharp rise vs. baseline | Possibly a broken client release |

## 5. What gets deleted or demoted to dashboards

- CPU, memory, load, GC, and thread-count thresholds.
- Single pod restarts. If they hurt users, P1 fires.
- Log-error-line counts.
- Queue depth with no demonstrated link to user impact.
- Anything in non-production environments.
- Any alert with no owner or runbook.
- Any alert nobody acted on in the last 90 days.

Keep these metrics on dashboards. They're what you look at *after* a symptom page.

---

## 6. Example implementation (Prometheus / Alertmanager)

The `3d` example below is built from 5-minute recordings of the numerator and denominator, so it stays traffic-weighted and cheap to evaluate. Build the other long windows the same way, or use Sloth or Pyrra to generate the rules.

```yaml
groups:
- name: web-slo-recordings
  rules:
  - record: web:sli_bad:rate5m
    expr: sum(rate(lb_requests_total{service="web",class="bad"}[5m]))
  - record: web:sli_valid:rate5m
    expr: sum(rate(lb_requests_total{service="web",class="valid"}[5m]))
  - record: web:sli_error:ratio_rate5m
    expr: web:sli_bad:rate5m / web:sli_valid:rate5m
  # Build 30m, 1h, 2h, 6h, 1d, 3d the same way, e.g.:
  - record: web:sli_error:ratio_rate3d
    expr: sum_over_time(web:sli_bad:rate5m[3d]) / sum_over_time(web:sli_valid:rate5m[3d])
  - record: web:sli_bad:increase5m
    expr: sum(increase(lb_requests_total{service="web",class="bad"}[5m]))
  - record: web:sli_bad:increase30m
    expr: sum(increase(lb_requests_total{service="web",class="bad"}[30m]))

- name: web-slo-alerts
  rules:
  - alert: WebSLOBurnFast
    expr: |
      web:sli_error:ratio_rate1h > (14.4 * 0.001)
      and web:sli_error:ratio_rate5m > (14.4 * 0.001)
      and web:sli_bad:increase5m >= 10
    labels: {severity: page, service: web}
    annotations:
      summary: "web burning error budget at >=14.4x"
      runbook: "https://runbooks/web/slo-burn"
      dashboard: "https://grafana/d/web-slo"

  - alert: WebSLOBurnMedium
    expr: |
      web:sli_error:ratio_rate6h > (6 * 0.001)
      and web:sli_error:ratio_rate30m > (6 * 0.001)
      and web:sli_bad:increase30m >= 20
    labels: {severity: page, service: web}
    annotations: {runbook: "https://runbooks/web/slo-burn", dashboard: "https://grafana/d/web-slo"}

  - alert: WebSLOBurnSlow
    expr: |
      (web:sli_error:ratio_rate1d > (3 * 0.001) and web:sli_error:ratio_rate2h > (3 * 0.001))
      or
      (web:sli_error:ratio_rate3d > 0.001 and web:sli_error:ratio_rate6h > 0.001)
    labels: {severity: ticket, service: web}
```

**Rule settings:** use no `for:` clause, or at most `for: 1m`. The windows already smooth the signal, and a longer `for` only adds detection delay.

**Alertmanager routing:**

```yaml
route:
  receiver: ticketing
  routes:
  - matchers: [severity="page"]
    receiver: pager
    group_by: [service]          # one incident -> one page, across alert types
    group_wait: 30s
    group_interval: 5m
    repeat_interval: 4h
  - matchers: [severity="ticket"]
    receiver: ticketing
    group_by: [service, alertname]
    repeat_interval: 7d

inhibit_rules:
- source_matchers: [alertname="WebSLOBurnFast"]
  target_matchers: [alertname="WebSLOBurnMedium"]
  equal: [service]
- source_matchers: [severity="page"]
  target_matchers: [severity="ticket"]
  equal: [service]
- source_matchers: [alertname="WebProbeFailure"]
  target_matchers: [alertname="WebTrafficCollapse"]
  equal: [service]
```

**Operational rules:**
- Only `severity=page` can reach the pager.
- Every page must carry a runbook link, a dashboard link, the current burn rate, budget remaining, and recent deploys.
- Maintenance silences are created by deploy or maintenance tooling, are time-boxed, and have an owner. Never use standing silences.

---

## 7. Rollout without missing outages

1. **Audit last week's 40 pages.** Tag each one as:
   - real and urgent
   - real but could wait (ticket)
   - duplicate
   - flap or self-resolved
   - not actionable (delete)

   This tells you which old rules to delete versus demote.
2. **Backtest** the new rules against 60–90 days of metrics. Confirm two things:
   - The 3 real incidents, and every recent postmortem incident, would have paged, and note how fast.
   - Total page volume is low: about 1–2 per week beyond real incidents.
3. **Shadow mode for 2 weeks.** New rules post to a Slack channel while old rules keep paging. Compare the two daily in both directions: what did each catch or miss, and which was earlier?
4. **Game day.** Inject each of these and confirm each pages or tickets exactly as designed:
   - a full outage
   - a ~5% error rate
   - a 0.5% error rate
   - a DNS break
   - a slow or hung backend
   - a single critical-journey failure
   - a killed Prometheus
5. **Cut over.** Demote old cause-based alerts to tickets for 30 days, then delete the ones that produced no action. Don't leave both systems paging.
6. **Watch nights and weekends** for the first month, and tune the minimum-event guards and the traffic-collapse floor there.

## 8. Keep it healthy

| Metric (review weekly) | Target |
|---|---|
| Pages per on-call shift | ≤ 2, ideally < 5 per week |
| Page precision (% needing urgent action) | ≥ 80–90% |
| Incidents found by customers or humans before a page | 0; each one is a detection bug with a postmortem action |
| Time to page for a full outage | < 5 min |
| Slow-burn ticket age | None older than 1 week |

**Tuning rules:**
- **A non-actionable page** must be fixed, demoted or deleted within the week. Whoever received it is empowered to do so.
- **A missed or late incident** usually means a missing journey SLI, a missing probe path, or a bad-event classification gap such as uncounted timeouts. The fix is rarely lowering burn thresholds.
- **Thresholds scale automatically with the SLO.** At 99.95%, replace 0.001 with 0.0005.
- **Revisit the SLI quarterly** for new critical endpoints, new failure modes, and changes in traffic shape.

---

## Summary

| Page (wake someone) | Ticket (business hours) | Dashboard / delete |
|---|---|---|
| Error ratio > 1.44% over 1 h **and** 5 m (14.4×) | > 0.3% over 24 h and 2 h; > 0.1% over 72 h and 6 h | CPU, memory, GC, load |
| Error ratio > 0.6% over 6 h **and** 30 m (6×) | Budget < 25% remaining or exhausted | Single pod restarts |
| Probes fail from ≥ 2 of 3 locations, 3 consecutive checks | Lost redundancy with the SLI healthy | Log-line counts, queue depth |
| Traffic < ~25% of the multi-week baseline for 10 min | Capacity > 75–80%, disk full < 7 days, certificate < 21 days | Non-prod alerts |
| Watchdog heartbeat lost / SLI metrics absent | Single-location probe failure, dependency degraded, p99 regression, 4xx spike | Anything unacted-on for 90 days |
| Disk full < 4 h, certificate < 48 h | Backup, cron or pipeline failures | |

**Expected result:**
- A full outage pages in about 1–2 minutes, and a 10% error rate in about 9 minutes.
- DNS, LB and routing failures are caught by probes and the traffic-collapse alert.
- Slow leaks become tickets days before the budget is gone.
- With about 3 real incidents a week, expect roughly 3–6 pages, each tied to real user impact, instead of 40.
results.notes: Well-structured with an explicit admission test, correct derivations, formal critical-journey and traffic-collapse pages with a multi-week median baseline; comparable rigor to A/C/D but shares the same unaddressed re-fire/inhibition subtlety.

## Recommendation

Use **opaque, stateful credentials**, with different delivery mechanisms for browser and mobile:

| Client | Credential | Storage | API presentation |
|---|---|---|---|
| SPA | Opaque session ID | `Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` host-only cookie | Automatically sent to a same-origin BFF/API facade |
| Mobile | Short-lived opaque access token | Memory | `Authorization: Bearer …` |
| Mobile | Rotating opaque refresh token | iOS Keychain / Android Keystore-backed storage | Token endpoint only |

Do not expose JWTs, access tokens, or refresh tokens to SPA JavaScript. Put the SPA and a BFF/API facade on the same origin, such as `app.example.com/api`. The BFF holds any downstream credentials and proxies API requests. This is the strongest browser architecture described by [RFC 10017](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc10017.html).

### Why opaque rather than JWT

Choose random, 256-bit opaque values and store only their SHA-256 hashes server-side.

This gives you:

- Immediate revocation for password changes, logout, device loss, or account suspension.
- No readable identity or authorization data leaking through the token.
- No stale embedded roles or permissions.
- One consistent place to enforce expiration, device/session status, and authorization changes.

JWT signatures do not prevent token theft; a stolen JWT is still a bearer credential. A JWT in `localStorage` is exposed to XSS, while a JWT in a cookie is exposed to CSRF and remains difficult to revoke. Once you add a JWT denylist or version lookup, most of its stateless advantage disappears.

The cost is an authorization-store lookup. Resolve opaque tokens at the API gateway and optionally cache positive results briefly. Revocation latency equals that cache lifetime, so use a small bound—such as 30–60 seconds—or bypass the cache for sensitive operations.

If independently deployed services truly cannot perform introspection, the fallback is a narrowly scoped JWT access token with a 5–10 minute lifetime, strict issuer/audience/algorithm validation, and no sensitive claims. Refresh tokens should remain opaque and stateful.

## Browser design

The browser receives only a cookie similar to:

```http
Set-Cookie: __Host-session=<random>;
  Secure; HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict; Path=/
```

Do not set `Domain`, and never store authentication material in `localStorage`, `sessionStorage`, IndexedDB, or a JavaScript-readable cookie. OWASP likewise recommends HttpOnly cookies or a BFF and warns against browser storage for credentials ([OWASP Session Management](https://cheatsheetseries.owasp.org/cheatsheets/Session_Management_Cheat_Sheet.html)).

The cookie references server-side session state:

```text
session_id_hash
user_id
device/session-family id
auth_epoch
created_at
last_used_at
absolute_expires_at
revoked_at
```

Use an inactivity timeout plus an absolute timeout. Reasonable starting points are 8–12 hours idle and 30 days absolute for “remember me,” shortened for sensitive applications. Rotate the session ID after login, privilege elevation, account recovery, and periodically during a long session.

There is no browser refresh token. Session renewal happens server-side, with the BFF rotating the session identifier when appropriate.

### Browser XSS

`HttpOnly` prevents JavaScript from stealing the session and replaying it elsewhere. It does **not** stop injected JavaScript from making authenticated requests while running in the victim’s page. Therefore also use:

- A restrictive CSP and Trusted Types where supported.
- Contextual output encoding and sanitization.
- No third-party scripts unless necessary; pin and monitor dependencies.
- Recent reauthentication for password, MFA, payout, or recovery changes.

### Browser CSRF

Cookies are automatically attached, so the BFF must explicitly defend against CSRF:

- `SameSite=Strict` where feasible; use `Lax` only where navigation or SSO behavior requires it.
- Require a framework anti-CSRF token or a custom, non-safelisted header on every state-changing request.
- Validate `Origin` and optionally Fetch Metadata headers.
- Allow credentialed CORS only from exact trusted origins—never `*`.
- Never perform state changes through `GET`.
- Make logout a CSRF-protected `POST`.

RFC 10017 explicitly requires BFFs to implement CSRF protection; SameSite alone may be insufficient when an attacker controls another same-site subdomain.

## Mobile design

Use Authorization Code with PKCE (`S256`) through the operating system’s external browser/authentication session—not an embedded WebView. This follows the native-app guidance in [RFC 8252](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc8252/).

Issue:

- An opaque access token lasting approximately 5–10 minutes.
- A longer-lived, single-use opaque refresh token.
- A separate token family for each app installation/device.

Keep the access token in process memory. Store the refresh token in Keychain or Keystore-backed secure storage. A hostile website cannot automatically attach an `Authorization` header, so ordinary browser CSRF does not apply to mobile API calls. PKCE, exact redirect matching, and transaction-specific `state`/`nonce` protect the authorization redirect.

For higher-risk applications, bind mobile tokens to an installation-held key using DPoP. That reduces off-device replay if storage is extracted, but it adds key-lifecycle complexity.

## Refresh strategy

On every mobile refresh:

1. Atomically consume the current refresh token.
2. Issue a new access token and a new refresh token.
3. Mark the old refresh token used while retaining its family relationship.
4. If an already-used token appears again, revoke the entire family and require login.

Serialize refresh attempts in the app so concurrent requests do not look like replay. Give refresh tokens both idle and absolute expiration—for example, 30 days idle and 90 days absolute—according to product risk.

Public clients must use refresh-token rotation or sender-constrained refresh tokens under [RFC 9700](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc9700/). Rotation provides detection, not just expiration.

## Password changes and security events

Maintain a monotonically increasing `auth_epoch` on each user. Every session and token record captures the epoch at issuance; reject it when it no longer equals the user’s current value.

For a password change:

1. Require recent authentication using the old password, passkey, or another strong factor.
2. Atomically increment `auth_epoch`.
3. Revoke every browser session and mobile token family.
4. Issue a fresh session only to the device that completed the reauthentication.

Apply the same policy to password resets, suspected compromise, administrative lockout, and significant MFA recovery events. This makes revocation immediate rather than waiting for access-token expiry.

## Logout semantics

Provide two explicit operations:

- **Log out this device:** revoke the current browser session or mobile token family, then clear the local cookie/Keychain token.
- **Log out all devices:** increment `auth_epoch` and revoke all session/token families, including the caller; then clear local state.

Server-side revocation is authoritative. Cookie deletion or mobile storage deletion alone is insufficient because a previously copied token would remain usable. Conversely, server revocation without clearing local state causes confusing retries.

Delete browser cookies using the same name, path, host scope, and security attributes with `Max-Age=0`. Push notifications or WebSocket messages may update other devices’ UI, but API rejection must enforce logout.

If authentication is federated, distinguish “log out of our app” from “log out of the identity provider.” Revoke your own sessions in both cases; initiate provider-wide logout only when the user explicitly requests it. OAuth token revocation and cascading grant invalidation are standardized by [RFC 7009](https://www.rfc-editor.org/info/rfc7009/).
